In Cangjie, 山 belongs to the 'shape class,' and it stands for the 'upward-open' form. Picture a valley or a basin: the mouth of it opens toward the sky, so every shape in this family shares that skyward-open look.

On the keyboard, 山 lives on the U key. The U key sits in the top row, seventh of ten counting from the left. The 卜 radical you learned earlier (the Y key) sits right beside it on the LEFT, and the 戈 radical you learned earlier (the I key) sits right beside it on the RIGHT. So next time you want 山, let your finger land just right of centre on the top row and you'll find the U key.

Let's see what the U key builds. Take 嘅, a character you write every day: it's coded RAIU. The mouth on the left is R, and the '既' part on the right breaks down until it finishes on that 山 shape — U. The character 號 is coded RSYPU, again ending on U. And 港 is ETCU, finishing once more with a press of U for that 山 form. You'll notice 山 often turns up at the tail end of a character as its closing code.

One last thing to remember: the U key doesn't only hide 山. It also holds two variant faces. The first is 凵, a shape that opens upward — you meet it inside 出 and 凶. The second is 屮, which looks like a little sprout just poking up, found inside 出. So these different-looking shapes are all, underneath, the very same U key.
U.zh:
睇下今日呢個字形：山。呢個字係一個象形字，畫嘅係三座山峰——中間高，兩邊矮，就好似你喺郊野公園望出去嗰道山脊咁。倉頡入面，山 屬於「字形類」，代表嘅係「向上開口」嘅形。你想像下：山谷、盆地，個口都係向上打開嘅，所以呢一類形都有個朝天開口嘅樣。

喺鍵盤上面，山 放喺 U 掣。U 掣坐喺最頂嗰行，由左數過去第七個位。你之前學過嘅 卜 部（Y 掣）就喺佢左手邊隔籬，而 戈 部（I 掣）就喺佢右手邊隔籬。所以下次你想打 山，隻手指喺頂行中間偏右嗰度摷一摷就搵到 U 掣喇。

我哋睇下 U 掣砌到啲乜。「嘅」字你日日都寫，佢拆做 RAIU：左邊個口係 R，右邊「既」嗰部分拆到最後，收尾就係個 山 形，打 U。「號」字拆做 RSYPU，同樣係以 U 收尾。「港」字就係 ETCU，最尾嗰個 山 形一樣係撳 U。你會發現，山 好多時都係擺喺字嘅尾段做結尾碼。

最後提你一樣：U 掣唔淨止收埋一個 山。佢仲收埋兩個變形。第一個係 凵，一個向上開口嘅形，你喺「出」同「凶」呢兩個字入面就見到佢。第二個係 屮，樣似一棵剛剛冒出嚟嘅芽，喺「出」字入面都搵到。所以呢幾個唔同嘅樣，其實背後都係撳同一個 U 掣。

V.en:
Look at today's shape: 女. You already know how to read this one — it means 'woman' or 'female'. Notice how its strokes twist and curl, bending like a ㄑ. In Cangjie, 女 belongs to the 'shape class', and the shape it stands for is exactly that twisting, curving stroke. Think of it as the 'twist' — a stroke that curls around on itself.

Now find it on your keyboard. The 女 shape lives on the V key, down on the bottom row, third from the left out of six. The 金 Metal shape you learned earlier sits right beside it on the left, on the C key; and the 月 Moon shape, also learned earlier, sits right beside it on the right, on the B key. So once you spot C and B, the one squeezed between them is the V key.

Let's see what the V key builds. The clearest example is 好, which opens with 女 — its code is VND, where that V is the opening 女. Do you see it? So many characters with a female or kinship flavour begin with this 女 stroke. Look next at 係, coded OHVF, and you'll find the V inside, standing for the 女 part. And 餐 is coded YEOIV, with the V tucked at the very end — again, that same 女.

The 女 shape is itself the very picture of a twist, so there's no separate disguised face to worry about here. Just remember: whenever you see that curling, bending ㄑ stroke, or a character opening with 女, reach for the V key. With a little practice it'll feel second nature.
V.zh:
睇下今日呢個字形：女。你一定識讀呢個字——「女」，代表女性、女人。留意佢啲筆畫係扭嚟扭去嘅，好似 ㄑ 咁一屈一彎。喺倉頡入面，女 屬於「字形類」，代表嘅就係呢種扭紋嘅筆——curling、curving 咁樣嘅一筆。你可以記住佢係「紐」，即係扭紋、扭曲嘅意思。

跟住喺鍵盤度搵佢啦。女 呢個字形擺喺 V 掣度，喺鍵盤最底一行，由左數起第三個。你之前學過嘅金（Metal）就喺佢隔籬左邊，即係 C 掣；而月（Moon）就喺佢隔籬右邊，即係 B 掣。所以只要你搵到 C 同 B，中間夾住嗰個就係 V 掣喇。

我哋睇下 V 掣可以砌到啲乜嘢字。最直接嘅就係「好」字，佢由 女 起筆，個碼係 VND——V 就係開頭嗰個 女。你見到冇？同女性、同親屬有關嘅字，好多都係由 女 呢一筆帶頭嘅。再睇「係」字，個碼係 OHVF，你可以喺入面搵到 V，代表當中嗰個 女 嘅部分。仲有「餐」字，個碼係 YEOIV，V 就收喺最尾，一樣係嗰個 女。

女 呢個字形，本身就係扭紋嘅代表，冇乜特別變身嘅樣。你只要記住：一見到扭嚟扭去、屈曲嗰種 ㄑ 筆,或者見到 女 字打頭,就諗起 V 掣。慢慢你就會覺得佢好熟手喇。

W.en:
Today's shape is 田, a paddy field divided into a grid. Take a look at the character 田: there's a box sealing it on all four sides, and inside, a horizontal and a vertical stroke cut the land into little squares — just like a real field ready for planting. But in Cangjie, this key carries an even more important job: it stands for the enclosure, the sealed box 囗 that wraps around things on all four sides. Look at 回, 因, and 國 — the outer box that closes each of them in. Whatever sits inside, that surrounding frame is the shape you're learning today.

You'll find this shape on the W key. Look along the very top row of your keyboard and count from the left: the second key is W, sitting up near the top-left corner. Since this is still one of your very first keys, there aren't any already-learned neighbours to anchor it to yet, so just remember it plainly: top row, second key, and pressing it gives you 田.

Let's see W at work. The character 個 is typed OWJR — notice the W in the middle, which is exactly the box on the right side of 個. The character 麵 is JNMWL, where that W again marks the enclosed box tucked inside. And 會 is typed OMWA, hiding another W within it. Little by little you'll notice that whenever a character has a squared-off, wrapped-around structure, W is usually involved.

Finally, here's its disguise: besides being the paddy field 田, W also shows up as the pure sealed enclosure 囗 — the outer box wrapping around 回, 因, and 國. So next time you spot a hollow frame closing something in, let it point you straight to the W key.
W.zh:
我哋今日睇嘅字形係 田，即係一塊分咗格嘅農地。你望吓個 田 字：四邊圍埋一個框，中間仲有橫豎兩筆將塊地劃成一格格，就好似真係喺田入面種嘢咁。不過喺倉頡入面，呢個鍵更重要嘅意義係——佢代表住個「方框」，即係四面圍住嘅框 囗。你睇「回」、「因」、「國」呢啲字，最外面嗰個圍起嚟嘅箱，入面裝乜嘢都好，個框本身就係我哋今日要學嘅字形。

呢個字形擺喺 W 掣度。你望吓鍵盤最頂嗰行，由左數起第二個掣就係 W 喇，就喺左上角附近。因為呢個仲係你頭嗰十幾個要學嘅字形之一，暫時未有隔籬已經學過嘅掣可以幫你定位，所以你就記住：頂行第二個，撳落去就係 田。

我哋睇吓 W 點樣砌字。「個」字打 OWJR，你留意中間嗰個 W，正正就係「個」字右邊嗰個框；「麵」字打 JNMWL，個 W 又係代表入面嗰個方框部分；「會」字打 OMWA，同樣藏住一個 W。慢慢你就會發現，好多字入面只要有個四四方方圍住嘅結構，多數都要撳 W。

最後同你講吓佢嘅變身：W 除咗係塊 田，佢仲會扮成純粹嘅方框 囗——就係「回」、「因」、「國」呢幾個字最外面嗰個圍住嘅箱。所以下次見到一個空心嘅框圍住啲嘢，你就要諗起 W 掣喇。

X.en:
We've finally reached the very last key — the X key. Unlike every other key you've learned, X doesn't stand for any shape. You won't find it inside any set of strokes, because it isn't a shape at all. X is Cangjie's escape hatch, its emergency exit. When a middle chunk of a character genuinely refuses to break apart — when there's no proper shape to represent it — Cangjie uses X to hold that spot. So what it represents is 難, meaning difficult: the difficult-to-split part.

Finding it on the keyboard is easy. The X key sits in the bottom row, the very first of the six keys in that row. Do you remember the 金 Metal key from an earlier lesson? Metal is the C key, and it sits right beside X, immediately to its right. So the neighbour just to the left of Metal is your X key.

There aren't many characters that use X, so you only need to memorise a handful. Look at 興: it breaks down as HXBC — the middle chunk won't split, so X holds the spot. The same happens with 與, coded HXYC, with X again filling in the middle. And 身 is simpler still, coded HXH.

These are special cases in Cangjie with no real pattern to follow, and the only way through is to learn them by heart. The X key doesn't come up often, but when you meet one of these stubborn, un-splittable characters, it's your lifeline. Congratulations — with the X key done, you've now completed all twenty-five Cangjie keys!
X.zh:
我哋終於嚟到最後一個掣喇——X 掣。同你之前學過嘅所有掣都唔一樣，X 唔代表任何字形。你唔會喺筆畫入面搵到佢，因為佢根本唔係一個形。X 係倉頡嘅「後備掣」，係一個逃生門。當一個字中間嗰橛真係拆極都拆唔到、搵唔到合適嘅字形去代表佢嘅時候，倉頡就用 X 頂住個位。所以佢代表嘅係「難」——難拆嘅意思。

喺鍵盤度搵佢好易。X 掣就喺最底嗰行嘅第一個位，六個掣入面排頭位。你仲記唔記得之前學嘅金（Metal）掣？金掣就係 C 掣，佢就緊貼喺 X 嘅右手邊。所以你搵金掣隔籬嗰個，就係 X 喇。

用到 X 嘅字唔多，你只要背熟幾個就得。睇下「興」字，佢拆做 HXBC——中間嗰橛拆唔到，就用 X 頂住。「與」字都係咁，拆做 HXYC，一樣係 X 喺中間補位。至於「身」字，就簡單啲，拆做 HXH。

呢啲字係倉頡入面嘅特例，冇乜規律可循，唯一嘅方法就係記熟佢哋。X 掣唔多用，但係遇到呢類拆唔開嘅字，佢就係你嘅救命掣。恭喜你——學完 X 掣，你就完成晒全部二十五個倉頡掣喇！

Y.en:
Look at this shape: 卜. It's just one dot sitting above one vertical post — two simple strokes we call 'dot-and-post'. That pairing might feel abstract, but it hides inside a lot of characters. One face of it is the lid 亠 — like a little cap worn on top of a character, which you'll spot above 交 and 市. Even more common is the walking road 辶, the sign for motion: any character about moving or travelling, like 迎, 這, and 過, carries it along the bottom.

Now find it on your keyboard. This is the Y key, sitting on the top row, sixth from the left out of ten. Since this is one of your very first keys, you don't have any learned neighbours to lean on yet — just remember it lives in the middle-right of the top row, and let your finger get a feel for where it sits.

Let's see what it builds. The character 號 is typed RSYPU, and notice how Y is tucked in the middle, standing for the dot-and-post part inside the character. The character 記 is typed YRSU, starting right off with Y — because the 言 element on its left wears the lid 亠 up top, so we lead with Y. And 餐 is typed YEOIV, also opening with Y, since the food element at its top hides this same shape.

Keep the two disguises in mind: one is the lid 亠, worn like a cap over 交 and 市; the other is the walking road 辶, hiding under motion words like 迎, 這, and 過. However different these faces look, the same Y key sits behind them all.
Y.zh:
睇下呢個字形：卜。就係一點加一豎，簡簡單單兩筆，我哋叫佢做「點豎」。你可能覺得咁樣嘅組合好抽象，但係佢喺好多字入面都收埋咗。頂帽 亠 就係其中一款——就好似戴咗一頂帽喺字嘅頭頂咁，你喺「交」同「市」呢啲字上面都見到佢。仲有一款更加常見嘅，就係行路底 辶，佢係「移動」嘅記號，凡係同郁動、行走有關嘅字，好似「迎」、「這」、「過」，底下都係佢。

喺鍵盤上面搵佢啦。呢個係 Y 掣，坐喺最頂嗰行，由左邊數過去第六個位。因為呢個係你頭幾個學嘅掣之一，暫時仲未有鄰居俾你參考，你只需要記住佢喺頂行中間偏右嘅位置，用手指去感受下佢喺邊。

我哋睇下佢砌到啲乜。「號」字打 RSYPU，你留意到 Y 收埋喺中間，代表咗字入面嗰個點豎嘅部分。「記」字打 YRSU，開頭就係 Y——因為「記」字左邊個「言」字部,頂上就係一頂帽 亠，所以由 Y 起手。「餐」字打 YEOIV，同樣係由 Y 開頭，個食字部頂上都收埋咗呢個形。

記住兩款變身：一款係頂帽 亠，好似「交」、「市」戴帽咁；另一款係行路底 辶，藏喺「迎」、「這」、「過」呢啲移動字底下。呢啲外貌唔同嘅形,其實背後都係同一個 Y 掣。

ch3-rule.en:
Today we learn one of the most important habits in Cangjie: split a character in the order you would write it. When you write Chinese by hand, don't you move left to right, top to bottom, and from the outside inward? Cangjie works exactly the same way. You break the character into little shapes, then take their codes in the same order your pen would follow — that way you never get lost.

There are two useful names to learn. In a left-right character — one block on the left, another on the right — the left block is called the 字首, the "head," and whatever remains on the right is the 字身, the "body." Keep these two names in mind; we'll use them throughout the book. When you take codes, you always take the head first and the body second, because that's the order you'd write them anyway.

Look at our first example, 明. At a glance you see it splits into two blocks: 日 on the left and 月 on the right. Following left-to-right order, 日 gives A and 月 gives B, so 明 is simply AB. Clean and tidy — two shapes, two codes.

Now look at 好, another left-right character. The left side, 女, is the 字首; the right side, 子, is the 字身. The head 女 gives a single code, V. Then for the body 子 we take its head and its tail — the top of 子 is 弓 giving N, and the bottom is 木 giving D. Put it together and 好 is VND. Notice the pattern: the head gives just one code, while the body gives head-and-tail. This is a very common arrangement.

As you practise, try "drawing" the character in your mind before you type — see where your hand starts, how it moves block by block — and split the codes in that same order. This feeling of "following writing order" becomes second nature the more you do it. One caution: sometimes, for the sake of compression, the dictionary's official code isn't quite what you'd predict, so treat your own guesses as exploration — the dictionary code always wins.
ch3-rule.zh:
今日我哋學一條好緊要嘅規矩：拆字要跟返你寫字嘅次序。你平時用筆寫中文，係唔係由左寫到右、由上寫到落、由外寫到入？倉頡拆字都係一樣。將個字拆做一嚿嚿嘅字形，然後照你落筆嘅先後次序取碼，咁就唔會亂。

先講一個重要嘅講法。左右結構嘅字——即係左邊一嚿、右邊一嚿——左邊嗰嚿我哋叫佢做「字首」，右邊剩返嘅叫「字身」。你記住呢兩個名，之後成本書都會用到。取碼嘅時候，一定係先取字首、再取字身，因為你寫字都係先寫左邊嘛。

睇第一個例，「明」呢個字。你一眼就見到佢分左右兩嚿：左邊係「日」，右邊係「月」。跟住左到右嘅次序，「日」取A，「月」取B，所以「明」就係 AB。乾淨俐落，兩嚿字形、兩個碼。

再睇「好」呢個字，佢都係左右結構。左邊嘅「女」係字首，右邊嘅「子」係字身。字首「女」取一個碼 V。到字身「子」嘅時候，我哋取佢嘅頭同尾——「子」個頭係「弓」取 N，個尾係「木」取 D。合埋一齊「好」就係 VND。你留意到冇？字首淨係俾一個碼，字身就取頭尾，呢個係好常見嘅安排。

練習嘅時候，你試吓喺落筆之前，心裏面「畫」一次個字，睇吓你隻手係邊度起筆、點樣一嚿嚿寫落去，跟住嗰個次序去拆碼。呢個「跟書寫順序」嘅感覺，練得多就會變成本能。要提醒你一句：有時字典為咗精簡，出嚟嘅碼會同你估嘅唔一樣，所以你嘅推測只係探路，最後一定要以字典入面嘅正式碼為準。

ch4-rule.en:
Last time we learned how to pick the head of a character. Today we look at the body. The body is whatever is left of the character, and it follows one very important rule: a body takes at most three codes — its first, second and last shapes. If there are many shapes crammed in the middle, you ignore them all and grab only the first, the second and the last. Fix this little chant in your head — head, second, tail — because it will stay with you for life.

Look at 信. This character splits cleanly into two parts: 亻 on the left and 言 on the right. The 亻 on the left is the head, and it takes one code, which is O. The 言 on the right is the body. When you look at 言, its shapes are 卜一一口 — four in a row. But a body takes at most three codes, so we grab only head, second and tail: head is 卜 (Y), second is 一 (M), and tail is 口 (R). The 一 in the middle is simply dropped. Put it together and 信 is OYMR.

Notice that 言 by itself actually has four shapes, but because it is serving as the body here, it gets trimmed down to just head, second and tail. This is the clearest possible demonstration of the head-second-tail rule.

Now look at 香. Unlike 信, this character does not split into a left and right part — it is an unsplittable "unitary" character. When you meet a whole character like this, you treat it as one lump and still take head, second and tail. The shapes of 香 are head ⽲ (H), second 木 (D), tail 日 (A), so 香 is HDA. As a side note, if a unitary character has four shapes or fewer, you simply take them all — no picking required.

When you practise, remind yourself first whether the character splits apart. If it does, separate the head from the body, then take head-second-tail from the body. If it does not, treat it as a unitary character and still take head-second-tail. And if the code table has one of its odd compression quirks, treat your own guess as exploration only — the dictionary code always wins.
ch4-rule.zh:
上一堂我哋學咗字首要點揀，今堂就講字身。字身就係一個字剩返落嚟嗰嚿嘢，佢有一條好緊要嘅規矩：字身最多只可以取三碼，就係第一、第二同埋最尾嗰個字形。中間如果有好多個字形，統統唔理，淨係捉頭、二、尾三個。你要記住呢個「頭二尾」嘅口訣，佢會跟你成世。

我哋睇「信」字。呢個字好清楚分做兩橛：左邊嘅「亻」同右邊嘅「言」。左邊嘅「亻」係字首，佢佔一碼，就係 O。右邊嘅「言」就係字身喇。你望住「言」，佢嘅字形係卜一一口，一連四個。但係字身最多只取三碼，所以我哋只捉頭、二、尾：頭係卜（Y），第二係一（M），最尾係口（R）。中間嗰個「一」就唔理佢喇。合埋一齊，「信」就係 OYMR。

你留意返，「言」本身其實有四個字形，但因為佢喺度做字身，所以就要斬件，只留頭二尾三個。呢個就係「頭二尾」規矩最典型嘅示範。

跟住睇「香」字。呢個字唔似「信」咁分到左右兩橛，佢係一個唔拆得開嘅「整體字」。碰到整體字，佢自己就當成一嚿嘢嚟取碼，一樣係捉頭、二、尾。「香」嘅字形係頭「⽲」（H）、第二「木」（D）、尾「日」（A），所以「香」就係 HDA。順帶一提，如果一個整體字四碼或以下,你就全部取晒，唔使揀。

練習嘅時候，你要提自己：先睇呢個字拆唔拆得開。拆得開就分字首同字身，字身再捉頭二尾；拆唔開就當整體字，一樣捉頭二尾。碼表如果有精簡嘅古怪情況，你嘅推測就當係探路，最終一定要以字典嘅碼為準。

ch5-rule.en:
So far, most of the characters we've met split cleanly into two chunks: one on the left, one on the right, as if there's an invisible line down the middle. These are called composite characters. In this lesson we learn a very important rule: inside a composite character, the head takes at most two codes — first and last — while the body takes at most three — first, second and last. Hold onto those numbers: two for the head, three for the body.

Let's look at 港. When you look at it, the left side is the three-drops-of-water 氵, and the right side is 巷. The left three-drops is the head, and on your keyboard it's E. Because the head takes at most two codes, but the three-drops is only a single shape, it simply gives one E. Now the body 巷 takes three codes — head, second, tail: the head is 廿, which is T; the second is 金, which is C; and the tail is 凵, which is U. Put together, 港 = ETCU. Try slowly rebuilding it chunk by chunk, and feel how 'two for the head, three for the body' actually works.

But what about a character that can't be split into two chunks? These are called unitary characters. A unitary character takes at most four codes: first, second, third and last — notice, you take the first, second and third, then jump straight to the very last, skipping over any extra shapes in the middle.

Let's use 為. 為 is a unitary character with no clear left-right dividing line. It takes four codes — first, second, third, last: the first is 戈 I, the second is 大 K, the third is 弓 N, and the last is 火 (the four dots underneath, 灬) F. Any leftover shapes in the middle get skipped. Altogether that gives 為 = IKNF. You'll notice that coding a unitary character is like standing in a long queue and only picking out the first three and the very last person.

When you practise, watch whether each character is composite or unitary: if it splits cleanly, use 'head two, body three'; if it can't be split, use 'first, second, third, last'. But also remember that the dictionary sometimes compresses codes — some characters actually take fewer codes than the rule predicts. So the code you build yourself is only an exploration, a guess, and the dictionary's code always wins in the end. That's exactly why the app never grades your predictions. Go ahead and try boldly — even guessing wrong is part of learning.
ch5-rule.zh:
到目前為止，我哋見過嘅字大多數都可以清清楚楚咁分開兩橛：左邊一橛，右邊一橛，好似有條隱形嘅界線咁。呢啲叫做分體字。呢一課，我哋要學一條好重要嘅規矩：分體字入面，字首最多取兩碼——即係頭同尾；字身最多取三碼——即係頭、二、尾。記住呢個數字：字首二碼，字身三碼。

我哋睇吓「港」呢個字。你望住佢，左邊係三點水 氵，右邊係「巷」。左邊三點水就係字首，佢喺鍵盤上面係 E。因為字首最多取兩碼，但係三點水本身只係一個字形，所以佢淨係出一個 E。跟住睇字身「巷」，佢要取頭、二、尾三碼：頭係 廿，喺鍵盤上面係 T；第二個係 金，係 C；最尾係 凵，係 U。合埋一齊，港 = ETCU。你試吓慢慢咁一橛一橛砌返出嚟，感受吓「字首二，字身三」係點樣運作。

咁如果一個字冇得分開兩橛呢？呢啲叫做整體字。整體字最多取四碼，係頭、二、三、同最尾——留意，係取頭、第二、第三，然後直接跳去最尾，中間多出嚟嘅字形統統跳過唔要。

我哋用「為」嚟睇。為係一個整體字，冇明顯嘅左右界線。佢取頭、二、三、尾四碼：頭係 戈 I，第二係 大 K，第三係 弓 N，最尾係 火（即係下面四點嗰個 灬）F。中間任何多餘嘅字形都跳過。合埋就係 為 = IKNF。你會發覺，整體字嘅取碼就好似喺一條長隊入面，淨係捉頭三個同排最尾嗰個出嚟。

練習嘅時候，你要留意每個字究竟係分體字定係整體字：見到有清楚界線嘅，就用「字首二、字身三」；見到冇得分嘅，就用「頭、二、三、尾」。不過亦都要記住，字典入面有時會精簡——有啲字實際取碼會少過規矩預測嗰個數目。所以你自己砌出嚟嘅碼只係一個探索、一個估計，最終永遠以字典入面嘅碼為準。呢個就係點解個 app 唔會幫你嘅預測打分。放膽去試，估錯咗都係學嘢嘅一部分。

ch6-rule.en:
Today we're learning how to split a five-code character. Once you reach five codes, the rule is beautifully simple: the head takes two codes, the body takes three codes, and two plus three gives you five. You can hold it in your head as one little phrase — "head two, body three." That's the basic five-code shape.

Look at the first example: 讀. On the left is 言, on the right is 賣. The left side 言 is the head, and it gives you two codes — 卜 and 口, which are Y and R. Then the right side 賣 is the body, and it must give you three codes. The way you take three from a body is "first, middle, last": the first shape is 士, which is G; the middle shape is 囗, which is W; and for the last, you jump all the way to the final shape of the whole body — the 八 sitting at the bottom of 貝 — which is C. Put them together and you get Y, R, G, W, C, that is YRGWC. Notice that even though the body has many strokes, you only take three codes: first, middle, last.

Now look at the second example: 謝. This one is interesting, because its body splits into two pieces of its own. When the body can be divided into two parts, the quota becomes 2·2·1: the head takes two, the first part of the body takes two, and the second part of the body takes only its final code. So 謝 splits into 言 as the head, giving 卜 Y and 口 R; the middle 身 as the first part of the body, taking its first and last shapes; and the rightmost 寸 as the second part of the body, taking only its last shape. The official code is YRHHI.

The key thing to remember is that 2·3 and 2·2·1 are really the same idea — the whole character takes at most five codes, the head always takes two, and whatever's left goes to the body. Whether the body splits in two only changes how you share out those three body codes.

One last thing to warn you about: the dictionary sometimes compresses codes (精簡), meaning some characters actually take fewer codes than the rule predicts. So the code you work out on your own is only an exploration, a guess — the dictionary code always wins. As you practise, just feel out how "first, middle, last" works, and keep an eye on whether the body splits into two. If you guess right, lovely; if not, check the dictionary and stay relaxed.
ch6-rule.zh:
我哋今日要學嘅，係五碼字嘅拆法。到咗五碼呢個位，個規則好簡單：字首取兩碼，字身取三碼，合埋就係二加三，共五碼。你可以將佢諗成一句口訣——「字首兩碼，字身三碼」。呢個係最基本嘅五碼結構。

睇下第一個例：讀。呢個字左邊係「言」，右邊係「賣」。左邊「言」係字首，取兩碼——卜同口，即係 Y 同 R。跟住右邊「賣」係字身，要取三碼。字身取碼嘅方法係「頭、次、尾」：頭一個形係「士」，即係 G；第二個形係「囗」，即係 W；最尾要跳到成個字身嘅最後一個形，就係「貝」下面嗰個「八」，即係 C。合埋就係 Y、R、G、W、C，即係 YRGWC。你留意到冇——字身雖然有好多筆畫，但係我哋淨係取三碼：頭、次、尾。

跟住睇第二個例：謝。呢個字有趣少少，因為佢個字身自己再分成兩截。當字身可以再拆做兩部分嘅時候，配額就變成二・二・一：字首兩碼，字身第一截兩碼，字身第二截淨係取最尾一碼。所以謝拆做「言」係字首，取卜Y口R；中間嘅「身」係字身第一截，取頭尾兩碼；最右邊嘅「寸」係字身第二截，淨係取佢最尾嗰個形。官方碼係 YRHHI。

你要記住嘅重點係：二・三同二・二・一其實係同一個道理——成個字最多五碼，字首永遠取兩碼，剩返嘅碼數就留畀字身。分唔分截，只係影響你點樣分配字身嗰三碼啫。

最後有樣嘢要提你：字典入面有時會出現「精簡」，即係有啲字實際取碼比規則預測嘅少。所以你自己拆出嚟嘅碼只係一個探索、一個估計，永遠以字典入面嘅碼為準。練習嘅時候，你就慢慢感受下「頭、次、尾」點樣運作，同埋留意字身有冇再分截，估中咗開心，估唔中就對返字典，唔使緊張。

ch7-rule.en:
Today we're going to learn a very special key — the 難 key, which lives on X on your keyboard. Why does this key exist? Because some characters have a middle section that is genuinely too tangled to break apart. You look at it and look at it, but you simply can't find a clean Cangjie root that matches. When Cangjie was designed, this problem was foreseen, so a "difficult" key was set aside: whenever you hit one of these un-splittable spots, you reach for X to hold that place.

There aren't many characters like this. 身, 興, 與, 齊 all lean on X to handle their awkward middle. Because the group is small, you don't need to agonise over how to split them — the most direct approach is simply to memorise them, and then you'll type them on sight.

Let's take them one at a time. First, 身, whose official code is HXH. Look at 身: both its head and its tail have a 丿, and 丿 in Cangjie is H. The middle really won't split, so we use the X 難 key to hold it. Put it together and you get the head H, the difficult X in the middle, and the tail H — that's HXH. See how the head and tail each take one H, while the middle is handed over to X.

Now look at 興, a character that is complex as a whole; its official code is HXBC. The top is ⺕, which takes H in Cangjie. The middle is a tangle that genuinely can't be split, so once again we use the X 難 key to stand in for it. The tail then takes two codes: ⺼ is B and 八 is C, giving BC. Strung together you get H, X, B, C, that is HXBC. Notice the pattern: the most troublesome spot in the whole character is always handed to X, while the other positions follow the normal rules.

When you practise, here's what to notice: don't spend too long trying to force-split that middle section, because it was designed to be un-splittable in the first place. Instead, get a feel for "take the head and tail as usual, hand the middle to X." And one more reminder — the dictionary sometimes applies compression quirks, so if the code you work out doesn't match the dictionary, don't panic. Always defer to the dictionary's code — that's the one that's correct.
ch7-rule.zh:
我哋今堂要學一個好特別嘅掣——「難」掣，佢喺鍵盤上面係 X。點解會有呢個掣呢？因為有啲字，中間嗰嚿嘢真係亂到拆唔開，你望嚟望去都搵唔到一個完整嘅倉頡字根去對應佢。倉頡設計嘅時候就諗到呢個問題，索性畀咗個「難」位你，遇到呢啲拆唔到嘅位，你就用 X 頂住佢。

呢類字唔算多，好似 身、興、與、齊 呢幾個字都係靠 X 嚟解決中間個難位。因為佢哋數量少，你唔使死記硬拆嘅方法，最直接嘅做法就係背熟佢，見到就識打。

我哋逐個字拆嚟睇下。先睇「身」字，佢嘅官方碼係 HXH。你望住「身」，佢頭尾都有丿，丿喺倉頡係 H。中間嗰嚿真係難拆，所以就用 X 難鍵頂住。咁樣連埋一齊就係頭嗰個 H、中間個難 X、再加尾嗰個 H，即係 HXH。你睇，頭尾各取一個 H，中間交畀 X，就搞掂。

再睇「興」字，佢係一個成個都好複雜嘅字，官方碼係 HXBC。個頭係⺕，喺倉頡取 H。中間嗰嚿亂碼實在拆唔到，所以又係用 X 難鍵去取代。個尾就取兩碼：⺼係 B、八係 C，即係 BC。連埋一齊就係 H、X、B、C，即 HXBC。你留意到冇，整個字最麻煩嗰個位，一律交畀 X 頂住，其餘位置照正常規矩取。

練習嗰陣，你要留意嘅係：唔好花太多時間去死拆中間嗰嚿嘢，因為佢本身就係設計成拆唔到嘅。你反而要記住「頭尾照取、中間交畀 X」呢個感覺。同埋要提你一句，字典入面有時會有精簡嘅安排，所以如果你自己拆出嚟嘅碼同字典唔一樣，唔使慌，一切以字典嘅碼為準——字典嗰個先係啱嘅。

faces-rule.en:
You've built quite a few characters by now, and along the way you've quietly learned something important: in Cangjie, one key can wear many faces. You don't have to treat these shapes as brand-new things, because they're really just the same thing dressed up differently.

Take 水, water. When it stands on the left side of a character, it shrinks down into 氵 — the three-drop water radical. It looks quite different, but in Cangjie it's still the water part, still typed with the 水 key. So the next time you spot 氵, don't panic — just tell yourself: this is water.

The same goes for 手, hand. Very often, when it sits on the left, the hand flattens and slims into 扌 — the hand radical. It looks squeezed and narrow, but at heart it's still a hand, still typed with the 手 key. You've already run into it many times in the characters you've built.

Then there's 人, person. When it stands on the left as a radical, it becomes 亻 — the single-person radical. The two strokes turn into one upright and one slant, and it looks smaller, but it's still a person, still typed with the 人 key.

I'm not going to make you drill these by rote, because you've already met them naturally while building characters. All we're doing here is gathering the most common ones together so they connect in your mind. As you practise, here's what to watch for: whenever you see a transformed shape, try to recognise its "true form" — which full character it really is. Once you can do that, you'll find there's far less to memorise in Cangjie than you feared.
faces-rule.zh:
你砌咗咁多個字，其實已經識咗一個好緊要嘅道理：喺倉頡入面，同一個掣可以有好多個樣子。你唔使當佢哋係全新嘅嘢，因為佢哋根本就係同一樣嘢嘅唔同打扮啫。

舉個例，個「水」字。當佢企喺字嘅左邊，佢就會縮身變成「氵」——三點水。個樣睇落好唔同，但佢喺倉頡入面依然係水部，用返「水」嗰個掣。所以下次你見到「氵」，唔好慌，心入面同自己講：呢個係水嚟。

「手」都係一樣。你寫嘢或者打字嘅時候，好多時個手會變成「扌」——提手旁。個樣扁咗、瘦咗，但佢骨子裡都係手，用返「手」嗰個掣。你砌過嘅字入面，其實已經遇過佢好多次喇。

仲有「人」字。當佢企喺左邊做部首，就會變成「亻」——單人旁。兩撇變成一企一撇，樣子細咗，但佢依然係人，用返「人」嗰個掣。

呢一課我唔會叫你死背，因為你砌字嗰陣已經自然咁見過佢哋喇。我哋而家只係一次過幫你溫返最常見嗰幾個，等你腦入面連埋一齊。練習嗰陣，你要留意嘅係：見到一個變形嘅時候，試吓認返佢嘅「真身」係邊個字。認得到，你就會發現倉頡冇你想像中咁多嘢要記。

keys-rule.en:
Today we begin learning Cangjie, and the first thing I want to give you is a reassuring idea. You might imagine you have to memorise thousands of Chinese characters before you can type — but that's not how this works. Behind Cangjie sits a rather clever idea: no matter how complicated a Chinese character looks, it can always be broken down into 24 basic shapes. Twenty-four, that's all. Once you know these twenty-four shapes, in principle you can build any character at all.

Each of these shapes lives on one key on your keyboard. That means you don't have to remember thousands of things — you only need to grow familiar, little by little, with these twenty-four keys and the shape each one stands for. When you type, you're really doing something like building with blocks: you look at a character, see which few shapes it's made from, and press those same keys.

So let me say this clearly: we are not going to ask you to cram and memorise by force. Rote memorisation is the most painful path and the easiest one to give up on. Instead we'll start with the most useful, highest-yield keys — the shapes that build the most characters — and learn from there.

Each lesson we add only a few new shapes, never dumping too much on you at once. And every time you learn a new shape, we immediately put it to work building real characters, rather than talking theory in the air. You'll recognise more characters as you go, and your fingers will slowly start remembering where things are. Bit by bit, looking at a character and splitting it into shapes will become instinct.

When you practise, here's what to notice: don't try to memorise all twenty-four at once. Instead, enjoy each little moment of "oh, so that's how this character is built." The shapes are your foundation — walk steadily on them, and everything that comes later will flow far more easily.
keys-rule.zh:
我哋今日開始學倉頡，第一件事想同你講嘅，係一個好安心嘅諗法。你可能以為要背幾千個中文字先識打字，其實唔係咁㗎。倉頡背後有個好聰明嘅諗法：無論幾複雜嘅中文字，都可以拆散做 24 個最基本嘅字形。二十四個，就係咁多。你識咗呢二十四個字形，理論上乜嘢字都砌得出嚟。

每一個字形，都住喺鍵盤上面一個掣度。即係話，你唔使記幾千樣嘢，你只係要慢慢熟悉呢二十四個掣，同埋佢哋各自代表嘅形狀。你打字嘅時候，其實係喺度做一件好似砌積木咁嘅事——望住個字，睇佢由邊幾個形砌成，再撳返嗰幾個掣出嚟。

所以我要同你講清楚：我哋唔會叫你死記硬背。死記係最辛苦又最易放棄嘅方法。我哋會揀最有用、砌到最多字嘅掣行先，由最高回報嘅形狀學起。每一課只加幾個新形，唔會一次過塞太多嘢畀你。

而且，每學到新嘅字形，我哋即刻攞嚟砌真字，唔會空講理論。你會一邊認得多啲字，一邊手指開始記得個位置。慢慢地，望字拆形呢件事會變成你嘅直覺。

練習嗰陣，你要留意嘅係：唔好諗住一次過記晒二十四個。你反而要享受每一次「原來呢個字係咁砌」嘅發現。字形係地基，行得穩，之後嘅嘢就會順好多。
